props.title: Strait-Jacket

sections.content: Strait-Jacket represents William Castle's savvy pivot into psychological horror following Alfred Hitchcock's success with Psycho (1960). Joan Crawford, in one of her later-career "hagsploitation" roles, delivers an unhinged performance as Lucy Harbin, an axe murderer released after 20 years in an asylum. The film's marketing brilliantly capitalized on Castle's showmanship - theaters distributed cardboard axes and had nurses stationed in lobbies, similar to his gimmicks for House on Haunted Hill (1959) and The Tingler (1959).

sections.content: Crawford's performance exists in fascinating dialogue with her role in Queen Bee (1955), showing her mastery of psychological instability. The axe murder sequences, while tame by modern standards, pushed boundaries for 1964 audiences and established a template for slasher films. Castle's collaboration with writer Robert Bloch, who wrote the novel "Psycho," creates a taut exploration of maternal trauma that would influence later films like Friday the 13th (1980). SUBHEAD: The "Psycho-biddy" Genre Explosion

Strait-Jacket helped cement the "psycho-biddy" or "Grande Dame Guignol" subgenre that flourished in the 1960s. Films like Hush...Hush, Sweet Charlotte (1964) and What's the Matter with Helen? (1971) featured aging Hollywood actresses in horror roles that commented on fame, aging, and mental instability. This trend provided meaningful late-career opportunities for classic Hollywood stars while creating a unique hybrid of psychological thriller and horror.
